explain: A container's processes make system calls straight into the host kernel, so any kernel bug reachable through those calls is a candidate. A VM's kernel is separate; escaping needs a bug in the hypervisor's narrower interface.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Runtime settings that switch the fences off
question: A team says their pod needs `privileged: true` only to change one network setting. What is the better request?
options: Disable seccomp but keep capabilities default
Keep privileged; it is the same thing
Use hostPID instead
Add only the specific capability needed (for example NET_ADMIN) and keep seccomp, AppArmor or SELinux on
explain: The Kubernetes docs advise granting specific capabilities rather than privileged mode, because privileged also removes seccomp and LSM confinement and grants every capability.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Service account tokens and cloud identity for pods
question: Five apps in namespace shop all use the default service account. An admin binds a Role allowing `get secrets` to it so one app can read its config. What changed for the other four?
options: All four can now read Secrets in shop, because they run as the same identity
Only if they mount the Secret
Only pods created after the binding are affected
Nothing, roles are per app
explain: RBAC grants rights to the identity, and all five pods share it. Give each app its own service account so a binding affects only the app that needs it.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Exposed dashboards, kubelets and Docker APIs
question: A self-built cluster's kubelets run with flags only, no config file, and `--anonymous-auth` and `--authorization-mode` are not set. Port 10250 is reachable from the internet. What can an unauthenticated stranger do?
options: Only list pod names
Run commands in containers through the kubelet API, since anonymous requests are allowed and authorization defaults to AlwaysAllow
Nothing, because port 10250 uses TLS
Only read node metrics
explain: The kubelet auth docs give these defaults: anonymous requests accepted, AlwaysAllow authorization. TLS encrypts the connection but does not authenticate the caller. This is the Hildegard entry point.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: A container is a process with a narrowed view
question: A process inside a pid namespace runs the equivalent of kill -TERM 1, aiming at its own init process, which has installed no SIGTERM handler. What happens?
options: The signal is delivered, pid 1 exits, and the kernel SIGKILLs the rest of the namespace
Nothing reaches pid 1: a namespace member may only signal its init process for signals that init handles
The signal is redirected to the host's pid 1
The kernel rejects the call because pid 1 is in another namespace
explain: pid_namespaces(7) says only signals for which the init process has established a handler can be sent to it by other members of the namespace, and that this holds even for privileged processes. It exists to stop a container accidentally killing its own init. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP are forced through only when sent from an ancestor namespace.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: Probes, Services and DNS: liveness is not readiness
question: An application takes 40 s to warm its caches. Its only probe is a liveness probe with initialDelaySeconds 10, periodSeconds 5 and failureThreshold 3. What do you observe?
options: The pod becomes Ready at 40 s, because liveness failures only affect traffic
The container is restarted at about 20 s and keeps restarting, because the budget is 10 + 3 x 5 = 25 s
The pod stays Pending until the probe succeeds
Nothing: the kubelet waits for a first success before it starts counting failures
explain: Probes at 10, 15 and 20 seconds all fail, which reaches failureThreshold, so the kubelet restarts the container and the clock starts over. The fix is a startup probe on the same endpoint: periodSeconds 10 with failureThreshold 30 allows 300 s, succeeds at 40 s, and only then lets liveness and readiness begin.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: A five-turn session: diffs, state and generated queries
question: Which turn in the session is a replace rather than an add?
options: T2 now only remote ones
T3 actually make it staff level
T4 drop the salary limit
T1 the first search
explain: Level already held senior and changes to staff, so it is a replace. T2 fills a null slot (add), T4 empties a slot (remove), and T1 is four adds onto an empty state.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Poking the chain: truncate it, break it, reword it
question: You suspect a model hides information in its word choices. Which intervention tests this most directly, and what result would support your suspicion?
options: Filler tokens; accuracy rises with more dots
Early answering; the answer is fixed at step 0
Adding mistakes; answers ignore the mistake
Paraphrasing; accuracy drops when the same content is reworded
explain: Encoded reasoning lives in the exact phrasing, so rewording the content while keeping its meaning should destroy it and cost accuracy. Lanham et al. saw no such drop. Filler tokens test hidden compute, not hidden encoding; the other two test post-hoc reasoning.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Building and scoring a CoT monitor
question: A monitor flags 2% of clean runs and catches 90% of hacks. Hacks occur in 0.5% of runs. About what share of flags are real hacks?
options: About 18%
About 90%
About 2%
About 50%
explain: precision = 0.005 x 0.9 / (0.005 x 0.9 + 0.995 x 0.02) = 0.0045 / (0.0045 + 0.0199) = 0.184. 90% is recall, not precision. At this base rate, false alarms outnumber real hacks more than 4 to 1.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Pinned host memory: the precondition for overlap
question: On which system does switching from pageable to pinned host memory help least, and why?
options: The laptop, because its link is slower so the copy dominates either way
Neither; the ratio is a property of the PCIe generation, not the host
The desktop, because a faster GPU hides the staging copy behind the kernel
The desktop, because its CPU runs the driver's staging memcpy fast enough that staging was not the bottleneck
explain: Pageable transfers were 5.369 GB/s on the desktop against 2.308 GB/s on the laptop, so the desktop's staging memcpy was already near link speed and pinning only added 1.15x there, against 2.50x on the laptop. The bottleneck being removed is host-side, which is why the benefit is a property of the host.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: CUDA Graphs: paying the launch cost once
question: You are capturing on a stream from cudaStreamCreate. During capture you call cudaMemcpy (no stream) to upload a small constant. What happens?
options: The copy is recorded as a memcpy node in the graph
The copy executes immediately and is simply left out of the graph
The capture graph is invalidated, and cudaStreamEndCapture returns an error and a NULL graph
Capture succeeds but the graph can only be launched on the legacy stream
explain: cudaMemcpy enqueues to the legacy stream and synchronizes on it. While a non-blocking-flagless stream is being captured, any use of the legacy stream is invalid, and synchronous APIs are therefore invalid too. An invalid operation during capture invalidates the capture graph, and cudaStreamEndCapture returns an error and a NULL graph.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Inside the forward pass: query and document attend to each other
question: Why can a search engine cache document embeddings for a bi-encoder but not intermediate document states for a cross-encoder?
options: Cross-encoder hidden states are too large to store
In a cross-encoder every document token attends to the query tokens in every layer, so its states differ for each query
Cross-encoders use random dropout at inference time
Bi-encoders use a different tokenizer that is deterministic
explain: Attention mixes query tokens into each document token's representation from the first layer on. A cache keyed by document would be wrong for every new query. Size is a secondary issue; dropout (randomly zeroing some activations, used only as a training regularizer) is off at inference.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: What cryptography promises, and to whom
question: A web form sends a price to the server over an encrypted connection, and the server trusts that price. A user edits the price in their own browser before sending. Which goal failed?
options: None of the cryptographic goals: the sender is the attacker, so the server must not trust client-supplied data
Confidentiality: the encryption was too weak
Integrity: the ciphertext was altered in transit
Authenticity: the server did not know who sent it
explain: The connection did its job: nobody in the middle read or changed anything. The attacker is the legitimate endpoint. Cryptography protects data between parties; it cannot make an untrusted party honest. That is an access control and validation problem.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Block ciphers: what AES actually does to 16 bytes
question: How many bytes does AES encrypt in one call of the block function, whatever the key size?
options: Depends on the key size
explain: The AES block is always 128 bits, which is 16 bytes. Key size (128, 192 or 256 bits) only changes the key and the number of rounds.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: When hashes break: MD5, Flame and the SHA-1 collision
question: Why could Flame's authors reuse Microsoft's signature instead of forging one?
options: The signature covered an MD5 hash, and their malicious certificate had the same MD5 hash as one Microsoft did sign
They stole Microsoft's private key
Windows did not check signatures
MD5 is reversible
explain: Signatures sign hashes. A collision means two different inputs share the hash, so one signature validates both. No key was stolen.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Diffie-Hellman: agreeing on a secret in public
question: Eve recorded p = 23, g = 5, A = 8 and B = 19. What does Eve still lack to compute the shared secret directly?
options: Either secret exponent a or b (a discrete log)
Nothing, the secret is A x B mod p
The value of g
Bob's public key certificate
explain: The shared secret is g^(ab). From public values alone Eve needs a discrete log; at 23 that is a table lookup, at 2048 bits it is infeasible.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Sound primitives, broken systems: how crypto use fails
question: A code review finds `if request_sig == expected_sig:` in a webhook handler that uses HMAC-SHA-256. Which reviewer question does this line raise?
options: What must never repeat?
Is anything secret compared?
Where does randomness come from?
Is the key used for one purpose?
explain: The expected HMAC tag is secret until the attacker has it, and `==` may stop at the first differing byte, so response time can leak how much of a guess is right. Lesson 8 covers the fix, `hmac.compare_digest`. Nothing here repeats or draws randomness.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Nonce budgets for AEAD: counters, random nonces, XChaCha, GCM-SIV
question: A queue consumer encrypts messages with AES-GCM using `counter += 1` held in memory, starting at 0 each time the container starts. Containers are restarted on every deploy. What is wrong?
options: Each restart reuses nonces 0, 1, 2 and so on under the same key
Nothing: counters guarantee uniqueness
Counters are predictable, and GCM nonces must be secret
AES-GCM cannot use counter nonces
explain: GCM nonces only need to be unique, not secret or unpredictable, so a counter is fine in principle. The bug is that the counter resets while the key does not. Persist the counter (or reserve blocks of it), give each container a distinct fixed field, or use random nonces with a budget or a misuse-resistant AEAD.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Randomness in practice: weak, shared and first-boot keys
question: A company builds a golden virtual machine image with the SSH host key already generated, then clones it 500 times. What is the risk?
options: None, because SSH keys are 3072 bits long
All 500 servers share one private key, so stealing it from any one breaks all of them, and clients cannot tell the servers apart
The servers will refuse to start
Only the first clone can use the key
explain: A key in an image is copied, not regenerated. Every clone holds the same private key. Generate host keys on first boot (after the entropy pool is ready) and remove keys from images.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Reviewing crypto code: safe APIs, tests and migration
question: NIST IR 8547 deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography after 2030. What design property in your own message formats makes that migration easiest?
options: Hard-coding the algorithm in each function for speed
Using the longest available RSA keys
A version field and key id in every message, with the algorithm chosen in configuration
Encrypting everything twice
explain: Versioned formats with key ids let new and old algorithms coexist during migration and let you rotate keys without guessing which one made a message. Longer RSA keys do not resist a quantum attack.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: From MMA atoms to TiledMMA and TiledCopy
question: Why do GMMA atoms on Hopper give every thread the whole A tile in their A layout instead of splitting it across threads?
options: Because Hopper has no registers for operands
Because wgmma reads A and B from shared memory through a descriptor built on the whole tile
Because CuTe cannot partition across 128 threads
To make every thread load A from global memory
explain: The docs explain that the GMMA descriptor is built on the full A or B tile in shared memory, so the ALayout maps every thread to the same tile (stride 0 in the thread mode) and CuTe checks that the shared memory layout is valid for a descriptor.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: CXL protocols, device types and the path of one load
question: Which statement about a CPU write to CXL memory is correct?
options: The OS takes a page fault and copies the page to the device
The device DMA engine pulls the data from host memory
Writes must use special non-temporal instructions
The store goes into the CPU cache; when the dirty line is later evicted, the host sends an RwD and the device replies with an NDR
explain: CXL.mem is plain cache-coherent memory from the core's point of view. Stores land in the cache; the eviction of a dirty line becomes a request-with-data message, acknowledged by a no-data response.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Three questions before you touch a system: law, permission, ethics
question: A client signs a test agreement covering 'all our cloud servers'. One server in the list is actually run by a hosting company on shared hardware. What is the right move?
options: Test it: the client listed it, so it is in scope
Confirm ownership and get the hosting provider's terms or consent before testing anything that is not the client's to authorise
Test it gently, at night, so nobody notices
Skip the agreement and rely on the bug bounty rules of the hosting company
explain: Only someone entitled to control a system can authorise access to it. A client's list proves what the client believes, not what it owns. Many cloud providers publish their own testing policies; read them and keep the result with the agreement.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The UK Computer Misuse Act, section by section
question: Under CMA section 5, which fact alone gives a section 1 offence a significant link to England and Wales?
options: The accused speaks English
The target server was in England at the time, even if the accused was abroad
The website uses a .uk domain name
The victim company is listed on the London Stock Exchange
explain: Section 5(2) gives two links for section 1: the accused was in the home country when acting, or the computer containing the targeted program or data was. A domain name or a listing is not on the list.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Export controls: Wassenaar and 'intrusion software'
question: A researcher in the US emails exploit details for a router bug to the router vendor's security team abroad, so they can fix it. Which concept in the 2021 BIS rule fits best?
options: Deemed export to an E:1 country
Vulnerability disclosure
Entity List designation
Intrusion software production
explain: The rule defines vulnerability disclosure as identifying, reporting or communicating a vulnerability to people responsible for remediating it, to resolve it. The 2017 Wassenaar change excluded such technology exchanges from the development-technology control.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Cover-ups and whistleblowing: Uber's CSO and Twitter's security lead
question: Why could Sullivan be convicted of misprision of a felony?
options: Because Uber's bug bounty programme was illegal
Because a security officer must publish every bug
Because the evidence showed the hackers committed a CFAA felony, Sullivan knew it, and took steps to conceal it instead of reporting it
Because the hackers were from another country
explain: The Ninth Circuit explained that misprision needs a completed felony by the principal (here unauthorised access under the CFAA), knowledge of it, and concealment. The NDA could not retroactively authorise the access.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The domain-weight update, step by step
question: A colleague's DoReMi port returns the domain weights from the final step instead of the average over steps. What is the likely effect?
options: The output is noisier and reflects only the end of training, while the method (following Nemirovski et al.) returns the average over the trajectory
None, because the weights converge to a fixed point after a few steps
Weights will no longer sum to 1
The proxy model will diverge
explain: Per-step weights react to one minibatch and keep moving as the proxy learns. The paper returns the average over all T steps, which is smoother and integrates the whole run, including the early phase when weights change most.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Fitting a mixing law: RegMix, data mixing laws, judging a mixture
question: Your linear regression over 5 domains recommends putting 100 percent of the budget on Wikipedia. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Wikipedia really is the best data and the other domains add nothing
A linear function over mixtures always has its minimum at a corner, so the pick reflects the model's form, not the data
The regression has too many runs and is overfitting
The proxy models were too large
explain: A linear function on the probability simplex is minimized at a vertex, a single-domain mixture. Mixture effects are nonlinear (the first few percent of a domain matter most), which is why RegMix prefers LightGBM and averages the top 100 predicted mixtures.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Curation inside a domain: quality filters from phi-1 to FineWeb-Edu
question: Your GitHub domain is full of auto-generated config files. Which tool addresses this directly?
options: DoReMi, by lowering GitHub's domain weight
A document-level quality filter that drops low-value files inside the domain
Raising the smoothing parameter c
Iterated DoReMi with more rounds
explain: DoReMi can only scale the whole GitHub domain up or down, which also cuts the good code. Removing specific bad documents is a curation job, like phi-1's educational-value classifier.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Worked example: binary search over animation keyframes
question: A teammate measures one cold lookup and finds SoA only 16% faster, so they conclude the split is pointless. What is the strongest reply?
options: The measurement must be wrong; SoA is always 4x faster here
Per-lookup misses are similar, but the searched data is 4x smaller, so across many lookups it stays cached and the gap widens
SoA only helps with SIMD, and binary search is not vectorized
They should switch to a linked list of keyframes
explain: A single cold lookup misses in both layouts on its first few probes. The benefit of a 512-byte index over a 2 KiB one shows up when many lookups reuse the same lines, which is how an animation system runs.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Classification: levels, impact and the high-water mark
question: A system stores public product photos (confidentiality not applicable, integrity LOW, availability LOW) and customer support chats (confidentiality MODERATE, integrity LOW, availability LOW). What is its FIPS 199 confidentiality?
options: NOT APPLICABLE, because most of its data is public
LOW, the average
MODERATE, the highest value among its information types
HIGH, because it is customer-facing
explain: FIPS 199 uses the high-water mark: the system's value for each objective is the highest among its information types. Volume and averages do not matter; the support chats set confidentiality to MODERATE.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Tokens and masks: taking real values out of systems
question: An attacker steals the full orders database of a shop that uses vault tokenisation. What do they get for card numbers?
options: The card numbers, because the token is an encoding of them
Random tokens that only the vault can map back to card numbers
Card numbers, but only the last four digits
Encrypted card numbers they can brute-force offline
explain: Vault tokens are random and the mapping lives only in the vault, so there is nothing to decode or brute-force in the stolen table. Vaultless tokens (FPE, AES-SIV) are different: anyone with the key can reverse them.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Where DLP acts: endpoints, email, web and cloud
question: Why deploy a new DLP blocking rule in simulation mode first?
options: Simulation mode is faster
Because blocking rules are illegal in some countries
To measure how often it would fire and on what, and tune precision, before it blocks legitimate work
Simulation mode encrypts the data
explain: Simulation applies no actions but records matches, so you can measure false positives on real traffic and fix the detector or scope. Turning blocking on first usually breaks business processes and drives users to unmonitored channels.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a data security programme, and practice
question: Which pairing of case and missing control is right?
options: Tea 2025: no TLS on uploads
Snowflake 2024: no field-level encryption
OPM 2015: no data classification
Morgan Stanley: no per-device certificate review or serial reconciliation
explain: Morgan Stanley's failures were vendor oversight, unreviewed certificates and missing inventory. Tea's was retention not enforced; the Snowflake thefts used valid credentials without MFA or network allow lists; at OPM, officials said encryption would not have stopped attackers with valid credentials.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Testing equivalence: bitwise, tolerance and the cache-hit test
question: Your equivalence test asserts allclose on the logits with atol = 1e-3 and it passes. What has it established about the generated tokens?
options: They must be identical, since the logits agree to within 1e-3.
Very little on its own: a 1e-3 tolerance only protects an argmax whose top-2 margin exceeds 2e-3, and near-ties are far smaller than that.
They are identical as long as the temperature is 0.
Nothing, because allclose is never a valid comparison for logits.
explain: A tolerance d on logits preserves the top-2 ordering only when the gap exceeds 2d. With atol = 1e-3 the test is blind to every position whose margin is under 2e-3, and near-ties can be around 1e-06. A tolerance is usable when it is paired with the margin distribution; the problem is the missing margin check, not allclose itself.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Making rare states common: faults, BUGGIFY and swarm testing
question: A teammate sets the network drop rate to 50% in every simulation run to "find more bugs". What is the likely effect?
options: More bugs found, since more faults always means more coverage
The cluster rarely makes progress, so the run explores a small, repetitive set of states
Determinism breaks, because drops are random
Nothing, because consensus tolerates any drop rate
explain: The FoundationDB paper explicitly tunes fault distributions to avoid an excessive fault rate that drives the system into a small state space. At 50% loss on every run the cluster mostly retries and times out; deep states such as long recoveries under load are rarely reached. Vary the rate per run instead.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Threat-modelling a pipeline: poisoned pipeline execution
question: In the fixed workflow, why does the deploy job also need the production environment, when it already has `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`?
options: The `if:` is cosmetic and GitHub ignores it
Environments make jobs run faster
The `if:` lives in the workflow file, which a branch can edit; the environment's branch rule and reviewers are enforced by GitHub outside the file, and the cloud role can require that environment
Environments are needed to use actions/checkout
explain: A condition written in the workflow is only as trustworthy as the file. A branch can delete it. Environment protection rules are settings the branch cannot change, and an OIDC trust on environment:production means the cloud refuses tokens from any other job.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: OIDC from CI, precisely: subject claims and environments
question: A job runs on a pull_request event and references the environment `staging`. What subject does GitHub put in its token?
options: repo:ORG/REPO:pull_request
repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/pull/1/merge
repo:ORG/REPO:environment:staging
repo:ORG/REPO
explain: GitHub's reference: the subject includes the environment name when the job references an environment, and includes pull_request only if the job does not reference one.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Scanners in the pipeline: Checkov, Trivy and zizmor
question: A developer adds `#checkov:skip=CKV_AWS_24` with no comment to silence the open-SSH finding. What should the pipeline enforce?
options: Nothing: skips are always fine
Delete all skip comments automatically
Disable CKV_AWS_24 everywhere
Skips must name a reason (and ideally an owner and an end date) and go through review like any exception
explain: Checkov's format includes a suppression comment after the check id. A skip without a reason is an unreviewed exception to policy.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a secure pipeline, a response plan, practice
question: A self-hosted runner is suspected of running attacker code. What is the right first containment step?
options: Delete suspicious files on it and keep using it
Take it offline and replace it from a clean image, then rotate every secret jobs on it could reach
Restart the runner service
Rename the runner
explain: A persistent runner can hide leftover processes and modified tools (the PyTorch case). Rebuilding from a known-good image is the only state you can trust; secrets that passed through it must be treated as stolen.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Sampling: predict every mask, keep the confident, remask the rest
question: LLaDA 8B Instruct, under pure diffusion sampling, gives very short answers on math benchmarks. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model was trained with a causal mask
The response length hyperparameter was set too large
Random remasking was used by default
Fine-tuning data padded with |EOS| makes tail |EOS| predictions highly confident, so low-confidence remasking commits them first
explain: Padding teaches the model that the tail is |EOS|, and low-confidence remasking commits the most confident tokens first. The fixes LLaDA used were to zero the |EOS| confidence or to sample block by block.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Making diffusion LMs useful: AR initialization, RL and remasking
question: Why does DiffuLLaMA keep the 'shift operation' when it turns LLaMA into a diffusion model?
options: Because bidirectional attention cannot work without it
Because the shift makes the KV cache exact
So that the pretrained output at position i keeps predicting the token at i + 1, reusing what the AR weights already learned
Because masked tokens must always be predicted from the right
explain: An AR model's hidden state at i is trained to encode the next token. Keeping that alignment means a masked token is read from its left neighbour's output, so continued training starts close to what the weights already do. Attention is fully bidirectional either way, and caching is unaffected.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Chunked prefill or disaggregation: when each one wins
question: An offline batch job summarizes millions of documents overnight. There is no latency SLO; the goal is tokens per dollar. Which design do the sources point toward?
options: Separate prefill and decode clusters on different GPU generations, mandatory for throughput
Colocated serving with chunked prefill to keep every iteration near the compute-bound point
Disaggregation over 25 Gb/s Ethernet to save NVLink
Disaggregation, because it always raises goodput
explain: Goodput only matters when there are SLOs. DistServe's discussion says that in throughput-oriented offline settings, chunked prefill with piggybacking (decode tokens riding along in the batch of each prefill chunk) may be preferred because it fills each batch to the compute-bound threshold. vLLM's docs also note disaggregated prefill does not improve throughput.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: NTFS and the master file table, record by record
question: Record 812 is marked free and its sequence number is 4. An entry in the NTFS change journal (lesson 6) refers to file reference 812 with sequence 3. What does that tell you?
options: The journal entry describes the same file that the record holds now
The journal is corrupt, because sequence numbers never change
Record 812 is a directory
The journal entry describes an earlier file that used record 812 before it was freed
explain: The sequence number increments each time a record is freed. Sequence 3 in the reference versus 4 in the record means the record has been freed since; the reference points to an older occupant.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: APFS: containers, copy-on-write and snapshots
question: You remove the internal SSD from an Apple silicon Mac with FileVault on and image it with a write-blocker. What do you have?
options: A readable APFS volume, because write-blockers bypass encryption
Encrypted data that stays unreadable without valid credentials or a recovery key
A blank image, because the SSD erases itself
A readable image as long as you image the whole container
explain: Apple documents that internal APFS volumes stay encrypted without valid login credentials or a cryptographic recovery key, even attached to another computer. A write-blocker preserves data; it does not decrypt it.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: SRUM and browser history: network use and what was visited
question: The suspect cleared their browser history. What can SRUM still offer?
options: Per-application, per-user network byte counts with timestamps, showing that the browser moved data
The URLs that were visited
The content of the uploaded file
Nothing, because clearing history also clears SRUM
explain: SRUM's Network Usage table records BytesSent and BytesRecvd per application and user. It does not record URLs or content, and the browser's clear-history function does not touch SRUDB.dat.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Trusting your tools: Cellebrite, Signal (2021) and validation
question: Which practice most directly addresses the risk that one tool misparses a crucial artefact?
options: Running the same tool twice
Using a newer computer
Hashing the report
Confirming the finding with an independent tool and against the raw data
explain: A second, independent implementation is unlikely to share the first tool's bug, and checking the raw bytes removes tool interpretation. Running the same tool repeats the same error; hashing the report only shows it did not change later.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: FreshDiskANN: inserts and deletes without rebuilds
question: In the toy consolidation, why do B's out-neighbors C and F become candidates for p?
options: Because they are p's nearest points
Because RobustPrune always adds every candidate
Because paths that ran p, B, C or p, B, F must be preserved by giving p a chance to link to them directly
Because C and F were on the DeleteList
explain: Algorithm 4 adds the deleted node's out-neighbors to the candidate set of each in-neighbor, so navigation through the hole is preserved. RobustPrune then decides which to keep: here C survives and F is covered by D.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: The DPO loss on one preference pair, with real numbers
question: A pair has policy log-probs chosen -30, rejected -20 and reference log-probs chosen -32, rejected -18, with $\beta = 0.1$. What is the DPO margin, and does the implicit reward rank the pair correctly?
options: -1.0, ranked wrong, because the policy gives the chosen answer lower probability
+0.4, ranked correctly, even though the policy still gives the chosen answer lower probability
+1.0, ranked correctly
0, because the reference and policy disagree
explain: Chosen log-ratio: -30 - (-32) = +2. Rejected: -20 - (-18) = -2. Margin 0.1 x (2 - (-2)) = +0.4, so the implicit reward ranks it correctly. Yet the policy itself still prefers the rejected text (-20 beats -30). DPO scores improvement relative to the reference, not raw likelihood; lesson 7 shows why this matters.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: ORPO and SimPO: dropping the reference model
question: A team must align a 7B base model on one GPU with tight memory and has paired preference data but no SFT checkpoint yet. Which method fits best?
options: DPO, because it is the most widely used
KTO, because it needs no pairs
ORPO, because it trains from the base model in one stage with no reference model
IPO, because it regularizes better
explain: ORPO combines the SFT loss with the odds-ratio penalty, so it needs neither a prior SFT stage nor a reference copy of the model. DPO, IPO and KTO all assume a reference (normally an SFT model) is available.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: How dual writes silently diverge, and how to contain it
question: A dual write does `old.increment(counter, 1)` then `new.increment(counter, 1)`, retrying the second call on timeout. After a week the new counters are slightly *higher* than the old ones. What is the most likely cause?
options: Clock skew between the two stores
A timed-out increment had actually been applied, so the retry applied it twice
The backfill copied counters that were already migrated
Last-writer-wins dropped some increments in the old store
explain: A timeout does not mean the write failed. Retrying a non-idempotent delta (add 1) after an ambiguous failure double-applies it. Writing the full current value read from the source of truth, or making the operation idempotent with a request ID, removes the problem.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Why run your tracing logic inside the kernel
question: Why is a kernel module a poor way to add ad hoc tracing to a production machine, compared with an eBPF program?
options: A module cannot read kernel function arguments
Nothing checks the module's code before it runs, so one bad pointer or endless loop can crash or hang the whole machine
Modules can only be loaded at boot time
Modules run in user space and are therefore slow
explain: Modules run arbitrary native code in the kernel with no load-time safety proof. eBPF programs are verified first (termination, initialized registers, in-bounds memory) and only then JIT-compiled and attached.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Maps: counting, histograms and timing in the kernel
question: Many CPUs increment the same counter. Why does bpftrace recommend @c = count() over @c++?
options: count() uses per-CPU slots, so concurrent updates never collide; @c++ is a non-atomic shared update that can lose increments
@c++ is rejected by the verifier
count() is faster to read than @c++
@c++ sends an event to user space each time
explain: Per-CPU maps make writes cheap and exact. The trade is that reading the value is slower, since every CPU's slot must be summed.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Integer-only inference: int8 multiplies, int32 accumulators
question: A team accumulates int8 x int8 products in an int16 register to save space. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, products of 8-bit numbers always fit in 16 bits
Sums overflow: one product can reach about 32,000, so two products can already exceed the int16 maximum
The zero point can no longer be represented
The scale M stops being in (0, 1)
explain: A single product fits in 16 bits, but the dot product adds hundreds or thousands of them. Jacob et al. use an int32 accumulator for exactly this reason. ONNX Runtime documents a related issue with VPMADDUBSW, an x86 vector instruction (AVX2, AVX-512) that adds pairs of 8-bit products into 16 bits and clamps on overflow.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Edge devices: the doors attackers now try first
question: FortiOS/FortiProxy has 15 KEV entries (12 ransomware-linked); F5 BIG-IP has 8. What can you conclude from these counts alone?
options: BIG-IP is about twice as secure as FortiOS
FortiOS should be banned
Little about code quality: KEV records exploitation that was found and reported, which also depends on how common and attractive a product is
KEV only covers network products
explain: KEV is evidence of exploitation in the wild, not a defect rate. Deployment size, attacker interest and who investigates all affect the count. Use it to decide what to watch and patch fastest, not to grade vendors on its own.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Ivanti Connect Secure, 2024: chained zero-days and a fooled checker
question: On 10 January 2024 Ivanti published a mitigation, with patches still weeks away. Which of these did applying the mitigation NOT do?
options: Remove webshells, modified files and stolen passwords from devices already compromised
Block the known route to the vulnerable endpoints
Reduce exposure while waiting for patches
Buy time for a planned rebuild
explain: A mitigation stops new exploitation by the known path. It does nothing about what the attacker already changed or took, which is why Volexity said a mitigation does not remedy a past or ongoing compromise.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Management interfaces: keep the admin door off the internet
question: Does BOD 23-02 require an agency to take its public VPN portal off the internet?
options: Yes, all VPN services must be internal
No. It covers management interfaces; the VPN service itself may stay public (other rules, such as patch deadlines, still apply to it)
Yes, unless the portal sits behind a separate policy enforcement point
No, because VPN portals count as cloud management interfaces, which are out of scope
explain: The directive defines a networked management interface as one meant exclusively for administrators. The user-facing VPN service is the device's job, so it is not in scope, although BOD 26-04 still sets its patch deadlines.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Overthinking: 901 tokens to say 2 + 3 = 5
question: Why do Chen et al. measure outcome efficiency instead of just counting tokens?
options: Token counts cannot be compared across tokenizers
Outcome efficiency rewards models for being short even when they are wrong
It separates tokens that led to the first correct answer from tokens spent after it, so a long but necessary trace is not penalized
It is the metric the models were trained on
explain: A 3,000-token AIME solution that is correct only at the end has efficiency near 1. A 900-token answer to 2 + 3 that was right after 39 tokens scores 4.3%. Raw length cannot tell these apart.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: L1: putting the token budget in the prompt
question: Why does the L1-Max reward multiply by correctness instead of adding a length penalty?
options: Multiplication is faster to compute during GRPO
So that brevity is only rewarded on correct answers, which prevents collapse into very short wrong outputs
Because GRPO cannot handle negative rewards
So that responses over budget always get reward 0 regardless of correctness
explain: The additive variant was ablated and collapsed to very short CoTs. With a product, a wrong answer earns 0 at any length, so shortening only pays when the answer stays correct.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Where a sensor sits: kernel callbacks, minifilters and network filters
question: A sensor driver wants to stop `invoice.exe` from ever running. Where can it do that?
options: In a post-operation file minifilter callback after the EXE is closed
In its process-creation callback, by setting CreationStatus to an error code
In the WFP network filter when the process first connects
In the console, once the alert arrives
explain: The process-creation callback runs before the new process starts, and the documented CreationStatus field lets the driver fail the creation. A network filter or console action can only act after the process is already running.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Worked configs: SwiftOnSecurity's sysmon-config and sysmon-modular
question: A sysmon-modular coverage layer shows ATT&CK technique T1055 as 'covered'. What can you conclude?
options: Every process injection on these hosts will be detected
Defender for Endpoint is no longer needed
T1055 events are now blocked
The config collects telemetry that may be useful for T1055; whether it records a given implementation, and whether any detection rule uses it, still needs testing
explain: The project's README states that ATT&CK mappings identify potentially useful telemetry and do not guarantee that every implementation is recorded or that a detection exists. Coverage of data is not coverage of detection.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control II: App Control for Business, drivers and LOLBins
question: Your App Control policy runs in enforce mode and you see a 3076 event on one laptop. What does that tell you?
options: The file was blocked
The policy failed to load
The file was allowed by the ISG
That laptop is still running an audit-mode policy (or an additional audit policy), because 3076 is the audit-mode would-be block
explain: 3076 is written only for audit-mode policies; enforced blocks are 3077. A 3076 on a machine you believe is enforced means a policy there is in audit mode, which is worth checking with CiTool -lp and event 3099.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Tampering and EDR killers: SUNBURST, BYOVD and AuKill
question: Which control stops AuKill's outdated Process Explorer driver from loading if the file is already on disk?
options: The ASR rule 'Block abuse of exploited vulnerable signed drivers'
Sysmon event 6
LAPS
The vulnerable driver blocklist or an App Control driver block policy
explain: Microsoft's ASR reference says that rule prevents writing vulnerable signed drivers but does not stop an existing driver from loading; the blocklist or App Control policy prevents the load. Sysmon only records; LAPS manages passwords.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Running edge detection and ON/OFF matching on the toy house
question: Which change to the toy pipeline would most directly avoid the minute-45 failure?
options: Raise the edge threshold from 30 W to 70 W
Use more clusters in k-means
Sample faster so the lamp-off and fridge-on events fall in different samples
Use the cluster median instead of the mean as each appliance's power
explain: The failure comes from two events sharing one sample. Faster sampling separates them into two clean edges (-60 then +120). A 70 W threshold would drop the +64 edge but also the lamp's real +51 ON edge, and the fridge would still have no ON edge at 45. More clusters or a median do not undo a merged edge.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Cleaning: Unicode, case, punctuation and legal suffixes
question: Which single step makes `Ｑｕａｎｔｉｘ` (full-width) equal to `Quantix`?
options: Case folding with casefold()
Unicode NFC normalization
Unicode NFKC normalization
Removing punctuation
explain: Full-width letters are compatibility characters. Only the K forms (NFKD, NFKC) apply compatibility mappings; NFC handles canonical equivalence only and leaves them unchanged. Case folding does not map full-width letters to ASCII.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Job titles: taxonomies, seniority and embeddings
question: Why store seniority in a separate field instead of making `Senior Software Engineer` its own taxonomy entry?
options: Taxonomies cannot store adjectives
So that an occupation filter matches every level, and level can be filtered independently, without multiplying entries per occupation
Because embeddings cannot encode seniority
explain: Combining occupation and level multiplies entries and splits recall: a filter for software developers would have to enumerate every level. Two fields keep both filters simple and avoid one taxonomy entry per occupation and level.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Delegated vs application permissions, and who may consent
question: Which grant should an investigator treat as the most dangerous in a review of consent grants?
options: User.Read delegated, consented by one user
Mail.ReadWrite as an application permission on a non-Microsoft app nobody recognises
openid and profile for a verified Microsoft app
Files.Read delegated, consented by one user
explain: Application permissions work without any user and cover the whole tenant, and write access lets the app change or send mail. Microsoft's playbook places app-only versions of the Mail permissions, and all write-capable app-only permissions, at the top of the review list.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Devices and the Primary Refresh Token: SSO bound to hardware
question: Storm-2372 obtained a PRT through a device it registered. Which response removes that foothold most directly?
options: Resetting the user's password only
Disabling or deleting the attacker-registered device in Entra ID and revoking the user's sessions
Enabling security defaults
Blocking the user's home IP address
explain: Microsoft lists disabling or deleting the device as invalidating its PRT. A password reset invalidates PRTs obtained with the password, but the device remains registered; revoking sessions clears the refresh tokens as well.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Taking over admins: help desks, MFA resets and rogue federation
question: After containing an Octo Tempest-style intrusion, which audit activity indicates persistence that survives resetting every compromised user?
options: User registered security info
Set domain authentication (a domain switched to federated)
Reset password (self-service)
Update user
explain: Federating a domain to an attacker's identity provider lets them sign tokens for any user in that domain, independent of user passwords. It must be found and reverted, and the federation settings of every domain reviewed.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: select and poll: readiness that costs O(n) per call
question: A proxy holds 50,000 mostly idle connections and wakes about 1,000 times per second. Which change cuts per-wakeup kernel work the most?
options: Switch from poll to select
Raise FD_SETSIZE to 65536 and keep select
Move to epoll so the kernel keeps the interest set and returns only ready descriptors
Call poll with a timeout of 0
explain: With poll every wakeup copies and scans 50,000 entries, so the scan repeats 1,000 times a second. epoll stores the interest set in the kernel once and each wait touches only ready items. select is worse (bitmap rebuilds, 1024 limit), and a zero timeout only turns waiting into spinning.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high
question: A teammate tried 40 reranker configurations on a 50-query public set and reports the best one improved nDCG@10 by +0.035 over the baseline. What is the most defensible next step?
options: Ship it, since +0.035 is larger than typical noise on 50 queries
Re-run the same 40 configurations on the same 50 queries with a different random seed to confirm
Score only the chosen configuration (and the baseline) once on a fresh query set that played no part in the choice
Report the average of all 40 configurations instead of the best one
explain: The +0.035 is a maximum over 40 noisy comparisons, so it is biased upward. In our toy, the best of 20 identical systems already gains about +0.038 on 50 queries from luck alone. Re-running on the same queries cannot remove that selection bias, and averaging all 40 answers a different question. A single evaluation on untouched queries gives an unbiased estimate.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Contamination: when test queries leak into training data
question: Which practice gives the strongest protection against both adaptive overfitting and contamination for a production search eval?
options: Averaging results over more public benchmarks
A private query set sampled from recent traffic, labeled in-house, read for a few pre-declared decisions and replaced on a schedule
Reporting results with five decimal places
Running the paired t-test with alpha = 0.01 instead of 0.05
explain: Recent private queries cannot be in a model's training data and have not been tuned against. Rotation keeps them from wearing out under repeated reads. More public benchmarks help external validity but stay exposed to contamination; stricter alpha alone does not address reuse.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: ASLR and PIE: moving the targets on every run
question: A non-PIE Linux executable runs with randomize_va_space set to 2. Which part of its memory is still at the same address on every run?
options: The main program's own code
The stack
The heap
Shared libraries such as libc
explain: Stack, heap and libraries are randomized. A non-PIE executable is linked for a fixed address, so its code stays put and remains a dependable source of reusable code. Building with -fPIE -pie lets the kernel move it too.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Memory tagging and hardened allocators against heap bugs
question: With random 4-bit MTE tags, a use-after-free happens to access memory that was re-tagged with the same value the stale pointer carries. What is the chance of this for one access, and what follows?
options: Zero: tags are never reused
1 in 16; the access is not detected, so MTE is probabilistic rather than a guarantee
1 in 256; the CPU detects it later
1 in 2; MTE only checks writes
explain: Four bits give 16 values. A random match goes undetected, which is why MTE is described as a strong probabilistic mitigation, and why allocators choose tags to differ from neighbours where they can.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: What each mitigation does not stop, and where to practise
question: Which pair of mitigations, combined, covers both the return-address hijack and the function-pointer hijack of earlier lessons?
options: Stack canary and ASLR
A shadow stack (or PAC return signing) plus forward-edge CFI such as CFG or Clang CFI
NX and FORTIFY_SOURCE
Partial RELRO and a sandbox
explain: Shadow stacks and PAC guard backward edges (returns); CFI, CFG, IBT and BTI guard forward edges (indirect calls and jumps). Canaries and ASLR only hinder, and NX and FORTIFY address different steps.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Fixing it: pad, align, or stop sharing writes
question: Eight threads update a shared histogram with 1,000,000 buckets of 8 bytes; updates land on random buckets. What is the best fix?
options: Give each thread a private histogram and merge them at the end
Pad every bucket to 64 bytes
Align the histogram array to 64 bytes
Use a bigger cache line size constant
explain: Padding every bucket would turn 8 MB into 64 MB and wreck cache use for little gain, since random buckets rarely collide. Per-thread histograms (fix 1) remove shared writes entirely, at the cost of 8 copies and one merge. Aligning the array only moves where the boundaries fall.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Buying rounds with local work, and when that stops working
question: You halve B and keep E fixed. Which quantity changes the most?
options: Bytes uploaded per client per round, which doubles
SGD updates per client per round, which doubles
Rounds to the accuracy target, which always halves
The number of clients the server must wait for
explain: Updates per round are E times n_k over B, so halving B doubles them. Communication per round is set by the model size, not by B or E: one download and one upload of the parameters. Whether the extra local work converts into fewer rounds depends on how heterogeneous the clients are, so option C is exactly the trap.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: Why a filter breaks greedy search on an HNSW graph
question: A workload filters images by label 'cat' while queries are photos of dogs, so passing points sit far from each query. Which baseline suffers most?
options: Pre-filtering, because selectivity drops
Post-filtering, because the unfiltered search heads toward the wrong region
Neither, since both are exact
The oracle partition index
explain: This is negative query correlation. Post-filtering's unfiltered search converges near dog photos that fail the filter, and it must expand very far to collect K cats. Pre-filtering's cost depends only on how many records pass, not on where they sit.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Fine-grained experts: split each expert into m slices
question: You split each of 16 experts into 4 (64 experts total) but forget to change top-2 routing. What happens?
options: Per-token expert compute drops to one quarter, because 2 small experts are only half of one original expert
Nothing changes; the layer has the same parameters and FLOPs
Per-token compute rises 4 times because there are 4 times as many experts
The router stops working because softmax needs exactly 16 outputs
explain: Segmentation keeps compute constant only if you also raise the number of active experts from K to mK, here from 2 to 8. With top-2 of 64 quarter-size experts, each token uses 2/4 = 0.5 of one original expert instead of 2, a quarter of the FLOPs. Total parameters are unchanged.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Aux-loss-free balancing: steer the router with a bias
question: Why does Algorithm 1 use sign(e) rather than e itself?
options: The paper tried b += u x e and found it slightly better balanced but no better in perplexity, so it kept the simpler sign rule
sign(e) is required for causality
Using e would make the bias receive gradients
sign(e) guarantees exact balance every step
explain: Table 3 of the paper compares variants: the proportional rule reached MaxVio 0.028 to 0.040 with perplexity 9.51 to 9.53, versus 0.044 and 9.50 for the sign rule with u = 0.001. Neither variant involves gradients or future tokens.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-3: producer and consumer warps, then ping-pong
question: In ping-pong scheduling, what is warpgroup 2 doing while warpgroup 1 computes its softmax?
options: Waiting at a barrier until warpgroup 1 finishes
Running its GEMMs (PV of one iteration and QK of the next) on the tensor cores
Issuing TMA loads for the next K and V tiles
Computing its own softmax on the multi-function unit
explain: The barriers order the two warpgroups' GEMMs so that one warpgroup's slow softmax (exp on MUFU) lands under the other's tensor-core work. Loading is the producer warpgroup's job, and running both softmaxes at once would just make them compete for MUFU.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Why LLM serving needs its own attention engine
question: A decode step for Llama-style GQA with 32 query heads and 8 KV heads. Ignoring other effects, how much does GQA raise attention's operational intensity over plain multi-head attention with the same query count?
options: About 4x, because each KV head serves $g = 4$ query heads
Not at all, decode is always $O(1)$
About 32x, one per query head
It depends only on the page size
explain: The group size is $g = H_{qo}/H_{kv} = 32/8 = 4$. Each key and value loaded from HBM is reused by 4 query heads, so intensity becomes $O(g \cdot l_{qo}) = O(4)$. Page size changes how KV is addressed, not how often each byte is reused.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants
question: A batch has average query length 3 per request and GQA group size 8. Which query tile size does FlashInfer's heuristic choose?
options: 32, the smallest tile of at least 3 x 8 = 24 rows
1, because it is mostly decode
16, the smallest Tensor Core tile
128, the prefill default
explain: With head-group fusion the effective query length is $3 \cdot 8 = 24$ rows. The rule takes the smallest tile meeting or exceeding it among 1, 16, 32, 64, 128, which is 32. Choosing 16 would need two tiles; 128 would waste most of the rows.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Reflow and OT couplings: making the paths straight
question: A team has a large text-to-image flow model and a tight compute budget. Which is the main cost they accept if they choose reflow over minibatch OT-CFM?
options: Reflow changes the data distribution the model generates
Reflow requires simulating the first model to generate many training pairs and then a second training run
Reflow cannot be combined with Euler sampling
Reflow increases transport cost
explain: Reflow preserves marginals and does not increase convex transport costs, but each round needs a trained model, a large batch of ODE simulations to create pairs, and another training run. Minibatch OT only re-pairs samples inside each training batch.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: TLC: breadth-first search over every reachable state
question: TLC reports "Model checking completed. No error has been found" for the counter fixed with an atomic increment, with N = 3. What have you established?
options: Every behavior of the 3-process model satisfies Correct; larger N is unchecked
The fixed algorithm is correct for every number of processes
The Rust implementation of the counter is race-free
The algorithm terminates under every scheduler
explain: TLC is exhaustive only for the finite model you gave it, and only for the properties you listed. It says nothing about code, and termination was not checked (and without fairness it would fail). Proving all N needs a proof, for example with TLAPS, the TLA+ Proof System (the inductive-invariants lesson).

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Verus: proving Rust functions with requires, ensures and invariants
question: You delete the invariant line `triangle(n as nat) <= u32::MAX`, since the function's requires already says it. What does Verus report?
options: The assert sum + idx <= u32::MAX fails, because the loop no longer knows the bound
Nothing changes; loops inherit the function's preconditions
A termination error on the decreases clause
A borrow-checker error
explain: By default Verus verifies a loop in isolation, knowing only its invariant, so the precondition is forgotten inside the loop. Running it gives "assertion failed" (4 verified, 1 errors). The attribute #[verifier::loop_isolation(false)] opts out.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1
question: Without any scaling, which tensor type gains the most from E5M2 instead of E4M3?
options: Weights, because they are updated every step
Activations after LayerNorm, because they are near 1
Gradients, because their magnitudes spread over many more binades
None: both formats have the same range
explain: Gradients span a wide range of small magnitudes, so the extra exponent bit (about 32 binades instead of 18) matters most there. That is why the FP8 paper recommends E5M2 for gradients and E4M3 for weights and activations.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: When low precision fails: outliers, SwiGLU and debugging a run
question: Why did Fishman et al.'s FP8 runs diverge only after roughly 200B tokens?
options: The learning rate warmup ended at 200B tokens
Weight decay slowly aligns the two SwiGLU weight vectors in some channels; once aligned, their output grows quadratically and saturates FP8
E4M3 accumulates rounding error linearly with tokens seen
The data mixture changed at that point
explain: Their theorem and measurements show w1 and w2 aligning in outlier channels (correlation rising sharply between 125B and 210B tokens) while norms grow. Delayed scaling cannot anticipate the sporadic spikes, and the SwiGLU output saturates.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust and safety: what these teams defend
question: A script uses your public search page to download every seller's name, city and phone number, one page at a time, staying under your per-IP limit. No code is broken. Which OWASP automated threat is this?
options: OAT-008 Credential Stuffing
OAT-019 Account Creation
OAT-011 Scraping
OAT-001 Carding
explain: Scraping (OAT-011) collects application content or data for use elsewhere. Nothing is exploited: the search page works as designed, and the harm comes from volume and purpose. That is why abuse needs its own vocabulary outside bug lists.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Bots in business flows: ticket scalping and the BOTS Act
question: An attacker holds 50 accounts but only 3 payment cards and ships everything to 2 addresses. Your limit is 4 tickets per customer. With per-identity counting across account, card and address, at most how many tickets can they buy for one event?
explain: Each order must fit under the limit for every identifier it carries. Cards allow 3 x 4 = 12, but addresses allow only 2 x 4 = 8, and the tighter constraint wins. Per-account counting would have allowed 50 x 4 = 200.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fake accounts and Sybil attacks
question: A marketplace lets any new account list items for sale and receive payouts immediately. Fake sellers keep appearing. Which change best follows this lesson?
options: Require a CAPTCHA at signup
Ban email domains you have not heard of
Let new accounts buy freely, but require payout details and verification before selling, and hold early payouts
Require 16-character passwords
explain: Put the costly checks in front of the valuable action (selling and getting paid), and reduce value per success with holds. A CAPTCHA adds little cost; banning unknown domains hurts honest users.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: EMV chips, the 2015 liability shift, and fraud moving online
question: Between 2015 and 2016, according to the Federal Reserve, what happened to remote (card-not-present) card fraud in the US?
options: It fell from 4.6 to 3.4 billion USD
It stayed flat
It rose from 3.4 to 4.6 billion USD
It disappeared because of chips
explain: Remote card fraud grew from USD 3.4 billion to 4.6 billion while in-person fraud fell from 3.7 to 2.9 billion: displacement from the hardened channel to the open one.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fake reviews and content abuse
question: Two images differ in 1 bit of their perceptual hashes; their SHA-256 hashes differ in about half their bits. What does this tell you?
options: The images look almost the same (for example a re-encoded copy); a cryptographic hash is designed to change completely on any change
The images are unrelated
SHA-256 is broken
Perceptual hashes are cryptographic
explain: Perceptual hashes keep similar inputs close in Hamming distance; cryptographic hashes are designed so any change scrambles the output. That is why matching known media uses perceptual hashes.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
question: Spot the bug. A program writes `state.tmp`, calls `rename("state.tmp", "state")`, then fsyncs the directory. It never fsyncs `state.tmp`. What can a crash leave behind?
options: Nothing bad: the directory fsync also flushes every file in it
Two files named state
A durable name `state` that points to a file whose new data never reached disk, so it may be empty or partial
The old `state` file, always, because rename is atomic
explain: The directory fsync makes the rename durable, but it does not flush the data of the files it names. Without an fsync of the temporary file before the rename, the name can survive while the contents do not. Atomic rename only protects what other processes see while the system is running.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: What vulnerability research is, and the rules you work under
question: You find a crash by fuzzing a library on your laptop, then notice a company runs the same library on its public API. What is the right next step?
options: Report the bug to the library's maintainers privately, with your local reproducer
Send the crashing input to the company's API to confirm it is affected
Publish the reproducer immediately so users can protect themselves
Ask the company for a reward before telling them anything
explain: Your local reproduction is already proof. Hitting the company's API is testing a system you have no permission to test, publishing first leaves every user exposed, and demanding payment as a condition of reporting can be extortion. The maintainers can fix it for everyone, including that company.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing good harnesses: fast, deterministic and structure-aware
question: Your harness calls a function that writes a log line and appends to a global cache on every call. What two problems does this cause?
options: Logging slows every run, and the global cache makes later runs depend on earlier inputs, so crashes may not reproduce
None, as long as the program does not crash
libFuzzer refuses to compile code with globals
The global cache is counted as new coverage, which is good
explain: The libFuzzer docs ask for fast targets without logging and without global state. A cache carried between runs means a crash can depend on a sequence of inputs, and the saved single input will not reproduce it.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Measuring fuzzers honestly: coverage, crashes and statistics
question: Why did Klees et al. recommend the Mann Whitney U test rather than comparing average crash counts?
options: Fuzzing results vary widely between runs and are not normally distributed, so a non-parametric test tells whether a difference is likely real
It runs faster than computing an average
It counts unique bugs automatically
Averages cannot be computed for crash counts
explain: Run-to-run variance is large and skewed. Averages can differ by chance; the test estimates whether one configuration's results tend to exceed the other's, without assuming a bell curve.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Symbolic and concolic execution: solving for the input
question: A fuzzer stalls at the check `if (crc32(data) == header->crc)`. Why might symbolic execution also struggle here, while a FUZZING_BUILD_MODE build would not?
options: Solving for data that hashes to a given CRC through symbolic expressions of a whole loop is expensive, while the fuzzing build simply skips the check
Symbolic execution cannot handle any checksums
Fuzzing builds compute CRCs faster
SMT solvers do not support integers
explain: CRC32 is linear and solvable in principle, but expressed symbolically over a long buffer it is a heavy constraint. Disabling the check in a fuzzing-only build is far cheaper. For true cryptographic hashes, solving is infeasible.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Why exact matching fails and what an edit distance counts
question: A search box accepts any dictionary word within 2 Levenshtein edits of the query. For which query is this rule most likely to return junk?
options: `cat` (3 letters)
`restaurant` (10 letters)
`levenshtein` (11 letters)
All three are equally safe because the threshold is the same
explain: Two edits can rewrite 2 of the 3 letters of `cat`, so `cut`, `bag`, `act` and many other 3-letter words all match. For a 10 or 11 letter word, 2 edits keep most of the string intact. This is why search engines scale the allowed edits with term length (lesson 6).

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Indexes that skip most strings: trigram filters and BK-trees
question: In a BK-tree, the query is at distance 3 from a node and the search radius is 1. Which child subtrees are searched?
options: Only the child labelled 3
Children labelled 2, 3 and 4
Children labelled 0 to 4
All children, because 3 > 1
explain: Any match $u$ in a child labelled $i$ has $d(u,\text{node}) = i$ and $d(q,u) \le 1$, so by the triangle inequality $|i-3| \le 1$, giving $i \in \{2,3,4\}$. Every other child provably contains no match.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
question: A quad's code is (0.30, 0.40, 0.90, 0.20). What is the code of the same four stars if the labels A and B had been swapped?
explain: Swapping A and B turns the frame 180 degrees about (0.5, 0.5), so every coordinate becomes 1 minus itself. Here the original has xC + xD = 1.2, which is more than 1, and the swapped one 0.8, so the canonical labeling is the swapped one (then C and D trade places to get xC <= xD).

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: From an accepted match to a WCS header, and the triangle alternative
question: Groth's triangle matcher discards matched triangle pairs whose log perimeter ratio is far from the average. Why does that remove false matches?
options: False matches have larger perimeters
All true matches share one magnification between the lists, so their log perimeter ratios cluster, while false matches scatter
The perimeter is not scale invariant
It removes triangles with clockwise orientation
explain: Between two lists there is a single scale factor. Every truly corresponding triangle shows the same perimeter ratio; coincidental shape matches come from unrelated triangles of any size, so their ratios spread out. The same idea appears in Astrometry.net's scale-range check.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Better cells on the sphere: S2 cubes and H3 hexagons
question: How many cells does H3 resolution 2 have in total?
explain: c(r) = 2 + 120 x 7^r, so c(2) = 2 + 120 x 49 = 5,882. 122 is resolution 0 and 842 is resolution 1. The 12 pentagons are included in the count.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Warp and affine: an inverse map plus a border rule
question: A 5-tap filter on the row 10, 40, 90, 160 needs index -1 while computing output 0. Which rule returns 40 there?
options: REPLICATE
WRAP
REFLECT
REFLECT101
explain: REFLECT101 mirrors without repeating the edge, so index -1 maps to index 1, whose value is 40. REPLICATE clamps to index 0 and gives 10, REFLECT repeats the edge so it also gives 10, and WRAP folds to index 3, or 160. Only REFLECT101 reaches past the edge pixel to a real neighbour.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
question: You call torch.cuda.empty_cache() while a 3 MiB tensor is alive in a 20 MiB segment. How much of that segment is returned to the driver?
options: All 20 MiB, because only 3 MiB is in use
17 MiB, the free part
None of it, because the segment is split around a live block
3 MiB, the live tensor is moved to the small pool
explain: The allocator can only cudaFree a whole segment, and only when no block in it is in use. A partly used segment keeps all of its memory reserved, including the free 17 MiB.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Fixed-size suballocation for the KV cache, and diagnosing OOMs
question: A training job OOMs. memory_allocated is 30 GB, memory_reserved is 39 GB on a 40 GB GPU, and memory_summary shows 8 GB of inactive split blocks. What should you try first?
options: Enable expandable_segments to avoid stranded slivers in fixed segments
Call empty_cache() before every step
Switch to a smaller block size for the KV cache
Lower garbage_collection_threshold to 0.1
explain: 8 GB free inside split segments is fragmentation, which empty_cache cannot release because those segments hold live tensors. Expandable segments target exactly that; max_split_size_mb is the documented fallback.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts
question: All 32 threads of a warp read `s[7]` from a shared float array. How many passes does the access need?
options: 32, because every thread uses bank 7
16, because pairs of threads share a pass
1, because the word is broadcast
2, because reads of one bank are paired
explain: A bank conflict needs different addresses in the same bank. Here every thread asks for the same word, which the hardware broadcasts in a single pass.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return
question: After rewriting a kernel it runs in 0.62 ms instead of 0.90 ms, but its Memory Throughput row fell from 48 percent to 41 percent. What do you conclude?
options: The rewrite is a regression: the kernel now uses the memory system less efficiently
The measurement must be wrong, since less time with the same work implies a higher percent of peak
The rewrite is a 1.45x win; a SOL row can fall when the work itself shrinks, and duration is the thing you validate against
Nothing can be concluded without re-running with cache control disabled
explain: If the rewrite removed traffic, for example by fusing a pass or improving reuse, the kernel moves fewer bytes in less time, and the percent of peak can fall while the duration improves. The triage guide says to validate every change against absolute kernel duration for exactly this reason. The percentages are for classification, not scoring.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Warps and SIMT: 32 threads, one instruction, and divergence
question: A block of 256 threads executes `if (threadIdx.x < 96) heavy(); else light();`. How many of its 8 warps diverge on this branch?
options: 0: 96 is a multiple of 32, so the split falls on a warp boundary
3: warps 0 to 2 run heavy()
8: any if statement makes every warp run both paths
1: only the warp containing thread 96
explain: Threads 0 to 95 are exactly warps 0, 1 and 2; threads 96 to 255 are warps 3 to 7. Every warp's 32 threads agree, so no warp has to run both paths. Divergence is a per-warp property, not a per-block one.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
question: Why does increasing k (retrieving more chunks) not solve global questions on a 1-million-token corpus?
options: Because embeddings cannot represent questions
Because LLMs cannot read more than 10 chunks
Because chunks overlap by 100 tokens
Because the retrieved set is still ranked by similarity to the question and bounded by the context window, so it is a biased sample, not the whole corpus
